title: Circle Geometric Relationships
description: Use circle measurements, arcs, equal radii, and tangent relationships to find missing lengths and angles with Mark, relate, solve.

content.html:
The circle gives you relationships before you calculate

The move: Mark, relate, solve. Mark what the circle tells you, choose the matching relationship, then calculate.

Why it pays: A radius, an angle, or a tangent can supply information the question never writes as a number.

One caution: An arc measure is an angle; an arc length is a distance. Keep those jobs separate.

Start with the graph. The blue arc runs from the rightmost point A to the top point B. Trace the rest of the circle: how many copies of that arc make one full turn?

calculator.title: Compare the arc with the whole circle

content.hint: Trace equal copies of the highlighted arc around the circle. Compare one copy with the whole.
content.prompt: The highlighted arc runs between the two perpendicular radii. What fraction of the circumference does it cover?
content.solution: Four equal copies complete the circle, so this arc has one fourth of the full circumference.

calculator.title: Compare the arc with the whole circle

content.explanation: Four equal copies complete the circle, so this arc has one fourth of the full circumference.

content.html:
Mark, relate, solve

  1. Mark: locate the center, the given measurements, and the requested length or angle.
  2. Relate: use the clue: a whole-circle measurement, a fraction of a turn, equal radii, or a tangent.
  3. Solve: write the relationship with the numbers given, then calculate the quantity actually requested.

Start with the clue: do not choose a formula just because its letters look familiar.

You will use the same three steps as the clue changes.

Whole-circle clue: find the radius

A radius runs from the center to the edge. A diameter passes through the center and contains two radii.

\[d=2r,\qquad C=2\pi r,\qquad A=\pi r^2.\]

If the circumference is \(12\pi\), then \(r=12\pi/(2\pi)=6\). If the question asks for area, continue: \(A=\pi(6)^2=36\pi\).

Watch out: finding the radius may be a middle step. Circle the requested quantity.

content.hint: Use the circumference to recover the radius, then use that radius in the area formula.
content.prompt: A circle has circumference \(16\pi\) centimeters. What is its area, in square centimeters?
content.solution:
Mark the circumference and the requested area.
Relate: \(16\pi=2\pi r\), giving \(r=8\).
Solve for area: \(A=\pi(8)^2=64\pi\).
content.explanation: The radius is \(8\), so the area is \(64\pi\). The \(256\pi\) choice squares the diameter instead.

content.html:
Arc clue: use the fraction of a turn

A central angle has its vertex at the center. The arc it opens onto takes the same fraction of the circumference as the angle takes of a full turn.

\[\frac{s}{C}=\frac{\theta}{360}\]

Here \(s\) is arc length and \(\theta\) is the central angle in degrees. For radius \(9\) and angle \(80^\circ\), the circumference is \(18\pi\), so the arc length is \((80/360)(18\pi)=4\pi\).

Either direction: multiply by the fraction to find the arc; divide by the fraction to recover the circumference.

content.hint: Find what fraction of a full turn the central angle represents. The given length is that fraction of the whole circumference.
content.prompt: An arc cut off by a \(60^\circ\) central angle has length \(5\) inches. What is the circumference of the circle, in inches?
content.solution:
Mark: arc length \(5\), central angle \(60^\circ\).
Relate: \(60/360=1/6\), so \(5=C/6\).
Solve: \(C=30\) inches.
content.explanation: The arc is one sixth of the full circumference. Six copies of a 5-inch arc make 30 inches.

content.html:
Angle clue: locate the vertex

In the graph, O is the center; A, B, and C are on the circle. Angles AOB and ACB open onto the same arc AB, the arc that does not contain C.

  • At the center: the central angle equals its intercepted arc measure.
  • On the edge: the inscribed angle is half its intercepted arc measure.

Here the central angle is \(90^\circ\), while the inscribed angle is \(45^\circ\).

Check the vertex before halving: the location decides the rule.

content.hint: Recover the intercepted arc from the inscribed angle, then match the central angle to that same arc.
content.prompt: An inscribed angle measures \(52^\circ\). A central angle intercepts the same arc. What is the central angle, in degrees?
content.solution:
The inscribed angle is half its intercepted arc, so the arc measure is \(2(52)=104^\circ\).
The central angle has that same arc measure: \(104^\circ\).
content.explanation: The central angle is twice the inscribed angle when both intercept the same arc: \(104^\circ\).

content.html:
The other arc completes the circle

The minor arc is the shorter path between the endpoints; the major arc is the longer path. Together they make the full circumference, and their measures total \(360^\circ\).

If the minor arc measures \(120^\circ\), the major arc measures \(240^\circ\). With circumference \(18\pi\), its length is \((240/360)(18\pi)=12\pi\).

Name the requested path: use the angle for that arc, or subtract the other arc length from the circumference.

content.hint: Find the angle left for the longer path, then apply its fraction to the full circumference.
content.prompt: A circle has radius \(6\). A minor arc measures \(90^\circ\). What is the length of the corresponding major arc?
content.solution:
The circumference is \(2\pi(6)=12\pi\).
The major arc measures \(360-90=270^\circ\).
Its length is \((270/360)(12\pi)=9\pi\).
content.explanation: The major arc is three fourths of the circle, so its length is \(9\pi\). The \(3\pi\) choice measures the minor arc.

content.html:
If the arc angle is in radians, keep it there

A full turn is \(2\pi\) radians. Use the same fraction-of-a-turn idea:

\[s=\frac{\theta}{2\pi}(2\pi r)=r\theta.\]

For radius \(6\) and central angle \(\pi/3\) radians, \(s=6(\pi/3)=2\pi\).

Units decide: \(s=r\theta\) uses a central angle in radians. For a degree angle, use its fraction of \(360\).

No angle conversion is needed for either route.

content.hint: The angle is already in radians. Multiply the radius by the given central angle.
content.prompt: A circle has radius \(8\). What is the length of an arc with central angle \(3\pi/4\) radians?
content.solution:
Use \(s=r\theta\) because the central angle is in radians.
\(s=8(3\pi/4)=6\pi\).
content.explanation: Keeping the angle in radians gives \(6\pi\) directly. No conversion step is necessary.

content.html:
Triangle clue: mark the radii equal

O is the center, and A and B lie on the circle. Both OA and OB are radii, so triangle AOB is isosceles: its base angles at A and B are equal.

The marked radii in this graph are perpendicular, so the central angle is \(90^\circ\). The two base angles share the remaining \(180-90=90^\circ\). Each is \(45^\circ\).

Mark before solving: two radii give two equal sides and two equal base angles. Use the given angle measures, not the apparent size of a drawing.

content.hint: Mark the two radii equal, then identify the second base angle before using the triangle total.
content.prompt: O is the center of a circle, and A and B lie on it. If \(\angle OAB=38^\circ\), what is \(\angle AOB\), in degrees?
content.solution:
Because \(OA=OB\), both base angles are \(38^\circ\).
The central angle is \(180-38-38=104^\circ\).
content.explanation: The two equal base angles use \(76^\circ\), leaving \(104^\circ\) at the center.

content.html:
Tangent clue: draw the radius to the contact point

A tangent touches the circle at one point. The radius to that point is perpendicular to the tangent.

In the graph, OA is a radius and AP is tangent at A, so angle OAP is \(90^\circ\). If \(OA=3\) and \(AP=4\), then the right triangle gives \(OP=\sqrt{3^2+4^2}=5\).

Use the contact point: that is where the right angle belongs. The side opposite it is the hypotenuse.

calculator.title: Follow the radius to the contact point

content.hint: Draw OA to the contact point. Locate the right angle and identify which given side is the hypotenuse.
content.prompt: PA is tangent to a circle at A. The circle has center O, \(OA=5\), and \(OP=13\). What is the length of PA?
content.solution:
The radius OA is perpendicular to tangent PA, so OAP is a right triangle.
OP is the hypotenuse: \(5^2+PA^2=13^2\).
\(PA=\sqrt{169-25}=12\).
content.explanation: The tangent length is 12. Adding the two given squares would incorrectly treat OP as a leg.

content.html:
Two tangents from one outside point are equal

In the graph, PA and PB are tangent segments from the same external point P. Their lengths are equal: \(PA=PB\).

If \(PA=2u\) and \(PB=3u-2\), set \(2u=3u-2\). Then \(u=2\), and either segment has length \(4\), matching the graph.

Return to the question: the value of a variable and the length of a segment may be different answers.

content.hint: Set the two segment expressions equal. After finding the variable, evaluate the requested segment.
content.prompt: Tangent segments PA and PB start at the same outside point P. If \(PA=3v+2\) and \(PB=5v-6\), what is the length of PA?
content.solution:
Equal tangent segments give \(3v+2=5v-6\).
Solving gives \(v=4\).
The requested length is \(PA=3(4)+2=14\).
content.explanation: PA is 14. Reporting 4 would stop at the variable instead of finding the segment.

content.html:
For area, split the tangent shape into two triangles

Join the center O to the outside point P. Quadrilateral OAPB becomes two right triangles, OAP and OBP.

Each has a radius and a tangent segment as its perpendicular legs. In the graph, each area is \(\tfrac12(3)(4)=6\), so the quadrilateral has area \(12\).

Use the right angle: radius and tangent supply the base and height. If the tangent length is missing, find it with the Pythagorean theorem first.

calculator.title: Split the quadrilateral into right triangles

content.prompt: A circle has center O and radius \(8\). Tangents PA and PB meet it at A and B, and \(OP=17\). What is the area of quadrilateral OAPB?
content.hint: Find the tangent length from a right triangle, then add the areas of the two right triangles.
content.solution:
The tangent length is \(\sqrt{17^2-8^2}=15\).
Each right triangle has area \(\tfrac12(8)(15)=60\).
The quadrilateral contains two of these triangles, so its area is \(120\).
content.explanation: The perpendicular legs are 8 and 15. Adding the two triangle areas gives 120 square units.

content.html:
Let the clue choose the relationship

The remaining problems will not name the rule for you. Mark the given information, relate it to the requested measurement, and solve.

If a problem combines clues, finish one relationship before starting the next.

content.prompt: A circle has center O and radius \(9\). Points A and B lie on the circle, and \(\angle OAB=40^\circ\). The length of minor arc AB is \(k\pi\). What is the value of \(k\)?
content.explanation: Equal radii make both base angles \(40^\circ\), so the central angle is \(100^\circ\). The arc length is \((100/360)(18\pi)=5\pi\), giving \(k=5\).

content.prompt: A circle question gives several lengths and angles. Which version of Mark, relate, solve keeps the work on track?
choices: Mark the requested measurement; choose a relationship from the given clue; calculate; return to the requested quantity.
Mark the requested measurement; choose a relationship from the drawing size; calculate; return to the requested quantity.
Mark the requested measurement; choose a relationship from the given clue; calculate; report the first value found.
Mark the requested measurement; choose a relationship from the answer sizes; calculate; return to the requested quantity.
content.explanation: The stated clues justify the relationship. The drawing size and the answer sizes do not. Finish at the requested quantity.

content.html:
One final circle

Take this one from the question to the answer on your own.

content.prompt: A circle has center O and radius \(5\). From a point P outside the circle, PA and PB are tangent segments. The perimeter of quadrilateral OAPB is \(34\). What is the length of OP?
content.explanation: The two radii total \(10\), leaving \(24\) for two equal tangent segments. Each tangent is \(12\). Radius OA is perpendicular to PA, so \(OP=\sqrt{5^2+12^2}=13\).

content.html:
Mark the clue. Make the connection.

Circle geometric relationships turn the information you are given into the measurement you need.
